review_items.rationale: The accepted proposition is a participant-eligibility condition on verification, not a claim that lack of communication instantly removes authority. s-verify-documentation explicitly assigns VerifyLeader confirmation to voters; s-verify-api says it ensures leadership and may prevent stale FSM reads. s-membership-contract separates nonvoters from election/commitment participants. s-verify-tests includes success with one disconnected peer among three voters, so neither unanimity nor eventual success is demanded. s-leader-loop and s-transfer implement a majority calculated only from voters. Three voters plus one nonvoter is a validated ordinary configuration (s-config-timing-check, s-bootstrap, s-repl-ownership), not forced recovery. Real bootstrap/election/application establish the selected context. No conflicting source authorizes nonvoter substitution for the missing voter in verification.
limitations: The expectation is the narrow implementation verification contract derived from documentation and API, not a complete formal definition of linearizable reads.
This execution does not show loss of actual leadership; absence of eligible verification support is the checked discrepancy.

review_items.rationale: The consumer obligation is necessary, not sufficient for authority safety. b-verify starts at self=1 and threshold=2, registers all peer workers (s-leader-loop); b-heartbeat and b-notify-replication drain a future registration into Boolean vote without suffrage (s-replication, s-match-notify). With both remote voter send loops paused before delivery and prior replies consumed, no voter can supply a notification for the new future. Only released nonvoter workers can provide the missing positive notification. The voter-only control reaches the same public endpoint. Freshness of replies, concurrent membership changes and authority loss might still invalidate a verification even when voter eligibility holds, and are separate conditions. Lease failure and negative replies remain valid rejection paths: main loop and timer run, only peer calls are finitely delayed, and the released receiver responses are not altered.
limitations: Cannot distinguish which nonvoter positive reply—ordinary append or heartbeat—first drained this registration. Both are sourced producers of the same Boolean fact, and the participant conclusion does not require isolating them.
Transport positive counts are an upper bound on consumed positive notifications; absence is sufficient for this forbidden schedule but arbitrary positive counts would not prove quorum consumption.

review_items.rationale: Inspected the fixed v1 plan and assurance_generated_test.go under direct-checks/2a3711628c58423587c2ef66f2df64ee and raw execution a5644db0464f44ccb5dfc352dcff28b0. The driver creates fresh stores and real NewRaft workers, bootstraps identical membership, waits for actual node-0 election and successful Apply, reads persisted LogConfiguration index 1, compares decoded and public membership, and requires CommitIndex to cover that entry. It does not rely on GetConfiguration().Index(), whose implementation returns a configuration without its index (s-getconfiguration-check). Peer AppliedIndex is only queued-application progress per s-dispatch; completed remote FSM application is unnecessary to participant eligibility. Pipelines are explicitly unsupported, leaving one serial append and one serial heartbeat loop per peer (s-replication, s-heartbeat). The gate records each loop only at its next call before delivery, so the preceding response and notifyAll invocation have completed; all six gates remain closed until admission. No snapshots are triggered in this short, non-compacted three-entry history and no other RPC supplies verifyFuture votes. Thus reset counters cannot erase an outstanding voter response capable of later notifying this future. The public VerifyLeader call precedes the admitted event; only the selected peer gate then opens. Actual receiver code fills response fields, wrapper counts positive successful returns by independent ServerID, and future.Error supplies success. Result event is not a prerequisite. The monitor explicitly admits via admission, correlates independent op identity, and requires prefix.term before admission.term; it does not equate changing state with identity. The implication success => remote_voter_reply avoids demanding success of a pending operation. Raw events 0/1/2 identify nonvoter prefix/admission/result with term 2, persisted configuration index 1, command index 3, success=true, voter_replies=0 and nonvoter_replies=3; state remains Leader. Events 3/4/5 independently identify the voter control: success=true, voter_replies=3 and nonvoter_replies=0. Both scenarios complete, parsing has no errors, and the runner evaluated both result events with matching prerequisites. Later command-timeout logs occur after result during release/shutdown, not in the violating identity before observation. The independent 600 ms cutoff, setup deadlines, deferred releases and shutdown do not depend on observing forbidden success. No_issue_found is scoped correspondence review of this actual artifact, not an independent proof or a general validation of the implementation.
limitations: Only the no-pipeline in-memory transport variant with finite selective delays and unchanged membership is executed.
Public successful verification is observed; a subsequent FSM read, competing leader election and committed-data inconsistency are not.
The source basis explains nonvoter notification consumption, but this test is not an isolated comparison of every potential cause of stale verification.
